title: Post-demo follow-up: token velocity verification & operational checklist
text:
Post-demo follow-up: token velocity verification & operational checklist

["From: Irene Choi <irene@redwood.ai>
To: Tom Reynolds <tom.reynolds@fastcart.com>
Cc: Marissa Cole <marissa@redwood.ai>, Karthik Iyer <karthik@redwood.ai>
Date: Tue, 11 May 2027 15:12:00 -0700
Subject: Post-demo follow-up: token velocity verification & operational checklist

Tom — thanks again for the demo earlier. Quick recap from our side and the lightweight asks we need to size an initial Dedicated pilot and validate SLOs.

Summary of what we heard on the call (please correct if I've missed anything):
- Primary surface: chat + short documents summarization in the customer support UI (streaming responses for perceived latency).
- Typical completion length: ~350–550 tokens (median ~420).
- Steady-state QPS (business-as-usual): ~18 QPS.
- Bursts: peaks up to ~220 QPS sustained for 3–7 minute windows during marketing events.
- Concurrent interactive streams: ~120 concurrent streaming sessions at peak (users that keep websocket open).
- Latency targets: interactive feel, p95 first-token < 350 ms, p99 end-to-end generation < 1s (you noted you can be flexible on p99 for large generations).

To size reliably we need the following from you (small, structured ask):
1) 48-hour sample of traffic with timestamps, prompt lengths, completion token lengths, and whether streaming was used. A CSV works; attached is a tiny template (redwood_throughput_template.csv).
2) Clarify if the peak numbers you quoted are 1-minute, 5-minute, or 15-minute rolling windows (you said a few minutes).
3) Top-50 unique prompts (or representative buckets) — helps us estimate batching gain and cache hit-rate.
4) Any strict p95/p99 guarantees required by SLAs or procurement (you mentioned p95 focus).

Preliminary ops checklist from our side (what we'll validate once you share the sample):
- Tokens/sec profile (tokens/sec per request distribution + aggregate tokens/sec per minute).
- Burst vs steady-state split and the peak window length (used to recommend reserved capacity vs autoscaling delta).
- Streaming behavior: first-token latency requirement vs tail latency for the full completion, and whether partial outputs can be dropped.
- Concurrency mapping: concurrent streams vs per-request concurrency (KV cache sharding, per-GPU kv cache limits).

Next steps / timeline:
- If you can share the 48-hour sample and top prompts by EOD Wed (5/12), Marissa will run a preliminary sizing and return an estimate within 48 business hours.
- We'll also include an initial cost/throughput tradeoff for quantized model variants and a recommended canary rollout plan.

Attachments: [Attachment: redwood_throughput_template.csv (csv)]

Thanks — happy to hop on a quick call if it helps.

— Irene Choi
Solutions Engineer | Redwood Inference
irene@redwood.ai | +1 (415) 555-0182

", 'From: Tom Reynolds <tom.reynolds@fastcart.com>
To: Irene Choi <irene@redwood.ai>
Cc: FastCart Engineering Team <eng@fastcart.com>, Marissa Cole <marissa@redwood.ai>
Date: Tue, 11 May 2027 17:04:00 -07:00
Subject: Re: Post-demo follow-up: token velocity verification & operational checklist

Irene — thanks for the clear summary. We captured a few more specifics while I was on calls; attaching a 48-hour export (fastcart_traffic_sample_48h.json) and a small breakdown below.

Key numbers (from our telemetry, local timezone):
- Steady-state: 16–20 QPS (typical weekday afternoon).
- Peak windows: 5-minute rolling peaks hit ~210–230 QPS on two marketing spikes last week (these last ~4–6 minutes).
- Median request tokens: 410; 75th percentile ~530; maximum observed ~1,200 (rare).
- Average completion tokens/sec (per-request): varies, but aggregate tokens/sec during steady-state ~9k tokens/sec; at peak bursts we observed sustained 85k tokens/sec across the fleet (this is pre-aggregation, includes some internal retries).
- Streaming: yes, we need streaming for the chat UI. First-token latency matters most for UX; we target p95 first-token <350ms and are okay with p99 end-to-end <1s for typical lengths. For very long completions (>800 tokens) we can accept higher tails.

Questions for Redwood:
- How do you recommend we map the 5-minute peak to provisioning (reserved GPUs vs aggressive autoscale)?
- Can you estimate the tokens/sec per GPU you use for the M-variant quantized model you recommended on the call?

Attaching the sample and a short readme. Let me know if you need anything else.

Attachments: [Attachment: fastcart_traffic_sample_48h.json (json)]

— Tom Reynolds
Head of Product, FastCart
tom.reynolds@fastcart.com

', "From: Marissa Cole <marissa@redwood.ai>
To: Tom Reynolds <tom.reynolds@fastcart.com>, Irene Choi <irene@redwood.ai>
Cc: Karthik Iyer <karthik@redwood.ai>
Date: Wed, 12 May 2027 08:23:00 -07:00
Subject: RE: Post-demo follow-up: token velocity verification & operational checklist

Thanks Tom — the sample is perfect for an initial pass. High-level interpretation and an initial sizing sketch below (we'll refine after a short synthetic run):

What the numbers imply
- Aggregate tokens/sec at steady-state (~9k tps) and peak bursts ~85k tps across your fleet. The key question is how bursty those tokens are within the 5-minute window (spikes every few seconds vs even spread).
- Median completion ~420 tokens suggests per-request work is moderate; streaming helps hide perceived latency but still counts toward token budget.

Preliminary sizing assumptions (conservative):
- Model: quantized LLM-M variant (8-bit/4-bit quantization profile we discussed).
- Measured tokens/sec per GPU (estimate): 12k tokens/sec sustained for generation-heavy workloads with streaming enabled and continuous KV-cache warm (single-model lane).
- Effective QPS per GPU in interactive workload (median 420 tokens): ~28–35 QPS (depends on batching and average prefix length).
- To cover steady-state ~18 QPS comfortably: 1–2 GPUs dedicated (we recommend 2 for headroom and cache residency).
- To cover 5-minute peak ~220 QPS: recommended approach is Reserved Capacity for baseline (2 GPUs) + capacity buffer via autoscale or short-term reserved burst (we estimate 6 GPUs total to hit ~220 QPS headroom with conservative padding). That maps to ~4 additional GPUs beyond baseline for peak windows.

Streaming & concurrency notes:
- Streaming first-token latency primarily driven by model cold-start and queueing. Continuous batching and a warm KV cache reduce first-token latency; we recommend pinning warm workers for the highest percentile users.
- For 120 concurrent streams at peak, ensure per-GPU concurrency limit and KV cache shard distribution. We'll run a synthetic of 120 concurrent streaming websockets to validate tail latency and memory usage.

Next operational steps (what we'll do after you confirm):
1) Run a 2-hour synthetic replay using your 48h sample (we'll simulate the exact burst cadence you sent) — target: measure p50/p95/p99 first-token and end-to-end for streaming.
2) Produce an initial cost/throughput tradeoff matrix (quantized M vs larger/smaller variants).
3) Draft a canary rollout: start with 1–2% traffic on Dedicated lane, 10% on autoscaled Hosted for spillover, and progressive increase with rollback triggers (error rate, p95 latency, token spend).

I've attached a quick workbook with the initial sizing math (initial_sizing_estimate.xlsx) and started a draft Google sheet with the test plan: https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1A2b3C-fastcart-sizing-draft

If that matches your expectations, we'll schedule the synthetic run for Thursday 5/13 and come back with results by EOD Friday.

Attachments: [Attachment: initial_sizing_estimate.xlsx (xlsx)]

— Marissa Cole
Performance & Reliability | Redwood Inference
marissa@redwood.ai | +1 (415) 555-0274

Marissa — this is great, thanks. The reserved+burst approach sounds reasonable.

We confirm: run the synthetic on Thursday and share the canary plan. I'll loop in procurement if your sizing looks close to our estimates so we can talk committed capacity.

I'll also share the top-50 prompt buckets by EOD today.

— Tom
